title: AMD Just Had Its Biggest Run Against Nvidia Since 1999. Can It Survive Earnings?
detail:
AMD Just Had Its Biggest Run Against Nvidia Since 1999. Can It Survive Earnings?
Kamina Bashir
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 12:06 PM PST 3 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AMD outperformed Nvidia by 53.2 percentage points over five trading days, according to The Kobeissi Letter. That is the widest gap between the two chipmakers since Nvidia went public in January 1999.

That lead met its first test on Friday, when AMD stock fell 8.75%. Nvidia's November 17 earnings report now sets up the next one.

How Nvidia's Leadership Crisis Fed the AMD Rally

AMD rallied 44.7% over the 5-day stretch while Nvidia dropped 8.5%, according to The Kobeissi Letter. The previous record gap, set in April 2016, stood at 49.9 percentage points.

So far this year, the AMD vs Nvidia gap is even wider. AMD stock has gained 149.4% since January 1, while Nvidia is down 12.7%, as of Friday's close. That puts the year-to-date gap at about 162 percentage points.

Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens

The run overlapped with growing scrutiny of Jensen Huang, who quit Nvidia as CEO on November 12. The company named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement.

AMD also gave buyers its own numbers to work with. Its third-quarter revenue rose 45% from a year earlier to a record $13.4 billion. Data center sales nearly doubled to $8.5 billion.

"AMD has been a major beneficiary of Nvidia's historic volatility," The Kobeissi Letter posted on X.

Friday's Sell-Off Hands the Next Move to Nvidia

The record run lost some ground in Friday's session. AMD closed at $534.06, down from $585.30, and slipped another 2.41% to $521.20 after hours.

AMD Stock Performance. Source: Google Finance

Chip stocks sold off as a group. The 10-year Treasury yield remained above 5% after October's producer price index. Rising yields tend to hit growth stocks hardest, since their value rests on profits expected years ahead.

Trading volume reached 48.6 million shares, nearly double the 3-month average. Analysts at The Motley Fool linked part of the drop to profit-taking after the surge.

The after-hours price now sits just above $514. BeInCrypto's AMD stock price analysis marked that level as the line that would break the bullish setup.

Nvidia earnings land on Tuesday after the US market closes. The company guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%. Analysts polled by LSEG expect about $109.2 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.48 per share.

The quarter closed on October 25, before Huang resigned, so the results will reflect his tenure. The guidance for the next quarter will be the first issued with Kress as interim CEO.

Solid results and guidance could draw investors back to Nvidia. A weak one could drag the whole chip group lower, AMD included, because Friday showed both stocks still trade together.

title: Jim Cramer has a strong take on Nvidia's next chapter
detail:
Jim Cramer has a strong take on Nvidia's next chapter
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 10:33 AM PST 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

For the first time in 33 years, Nvidia is being run by someone other than Jensen Huang, and some of the loudest voices in the market are already lining up behind the person filling his seat.

Jim Cramer, Ross Gerber, Daniel Newman, and Kevin O'Leary have all voiced support for interim CEO Colette Kress as the chipmaker enters a new chapter.

That backing arrives at a shaky moment. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at the open and were down about 5% by the time trading settled on Nov. 12, the day the company confirmed Huang's departure.

The big question now is whether Kress can steady the world's most closely watched AI company until the board settles on a permanent leader.

Cramer had already warned investors to prepare for a future without Huang, but once the resignation landed, his view shifted to backing the person now in the seat.

Why Cramer thinks Kress is the right call for Nvidia right now

Cramer did not hold back. Speaking on CNBC, he described Kress as a tough, "no-nonsense" executive who "runs with a steel fist." He added that "she is absolutely the one you need right now" because she commands authority and has no patience for nonsense.

His view is shaped by years of dealing with her directly. Cramer noted that Kress has led Nvidia's earnings conference calls and has been his main contact at the company, alongside Huang, for a long time.

Also read: Michael Burry has a surprising new take on Nvidia stock

Kress brings a long record to the job. She has been Nvidia's chief financial officer since September 2013 and held senior finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft, and Cisco before that.

She also holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. During her time as CFO, Nvidia's yearly revenue grew from about $4 billion to more than $200 billion, as reported by Al Jazeera.

Gerber and Newman point to Nvidia's deep bench

Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management, said he was "very pleased" with the promotion and called Kress "more than prepared and capable to help lead Nvidia." He also argued the company has "a deep bench of highly skilled leaders," adding, "It's their time to step up."

Newman, who runs Futurum Group, said Kress "has always impressed me in our conversations." He expects Nvidia's long-term leadership to be "much more of an operations-centric leadership team" focused on "maniacal execution," similar to what Tim Cook was to Steve Jobs at Apple. "There is no replacing Jensen," he wrote on X.

title: Apple's Market Value Grew From $350 Billion to $4 Trillion During Tim Cook's 15 Years as CEO. Here's What That Growth Curve Means for Apple's Next Chapter Under John Ternus
detail:
Apple's Market Value Grew From $350 Billion to $4 Trillion During Tim Cook's 15 Years as CEO. Here's What That Growth Curve Means for Apple's Next Chapter Under John Ternus
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 11:31 AM PST 5 min read
AAPL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

At the end of August, Tim Cook stepped down as CEO of Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), ending a highly successful tenure as the head of one of the world's largest companies. Tim Cook led Apple as it revolutionized the tech sector and became the world's first trillion-dollar company. Apple is now worth $5.2 trillion, up from just $350 billion when Tim Cook took over -- though it was worth about $4.6 trillion when Cook ended his tenure as CEO. What does that mean for Apple's new leader, John Ternus?

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

A tough act to follow

Tim Cook became the CEO of Apple in 2011, four years after the first iPhone was released. Apple's famous smartphone was already a hit, but Tim Cook oversaw the company's creation and launch of several other highly popular products, such as the Apple Watch and the AirPods.

Perhaps more importantly, Tim Cook transformed Apple's installed base into a massive cash-generating machine through millions of paid subscriptions across more than a dozen services. Apple's services segment is now its second-largest by sales, and it carries much juicier margins than hardware products. That's the business John Ternus is inheriting: a lineup of popular devices, an even more popular brand name, and a massive consumer technology ecosystem with more than 2.5 billion active devices in circulation.

Apple is a stronger company than it was in 2011, but it is also far larger and operates in a more competitive environment. Could John Ternus really deliver returns on par with those that shareholders saw under Tim Cook's tenure?

Almost certainly not. Apple could be worth over $60 trillion in 15 years if Ternus can pull that off. To put things in perspective, consider that the entire GDP of the U.S. last year was just under $31 trillion -- Apple would be valued at nearly twice that by 2041 if Ternus can match Cook's performance over this period. That's not happening, but that doesn't mean Apple's shares are no longer worth investing in. Let's consider some reasons why the stock remains attractive.

Apple's excellent prospects

Apple has been the best-performing Magnificent Seven stock this year. There are several reasons for that, and at least one of them matters a great deal for the company's prospects. Apple's iPhone 17, introduced last year, has become very popular and powered a strong renewal cycle. Partly thanks to this product, Apple's top-line growth in recent quarters has been much stronger than the company's average over the past three years.

title: Coca-Cola Has Paid a Growing Dividend for 64 Years. Here's the Income $5,000 Can Start You With.

Coca-Cola Has Paid a Growing Dividend for 64 Years. Here's the Income $5,000 Can Start You With.
Eric Volkman, The Motley Fool

KO
NVDA

Among the general public, Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO) is renowned for its classic, sweet, fizzy drink. Among investors, it's known as one of the steadiest and most reliable dividend payers in business history. Not only that, it regularly declares dividend raises, to the point where it's a Dividend King (one of the rare stocks that has lifted its payout at least once annually for a minimum of 50 years in a row).

There's nothing like getting paid regularly by a company for the simple act of owning its stock. Here's how much someone will earn with a relatively modest $5,000 "starter investment" in Coca-Cola.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Coca-Cola.

The first 50

At Coca-Cola's most recent closing price, $5,000 would buy 50 common shares of the company, with a bit of change left over (which no clever investor should spend on penny stocks, but that's a topic for another time). The current quarterly dividend is $0.53 per share, so that holding would earn $26.50 every payment cycle, annualizing to $106 in total.

In and of itself, that $106 isn't going to put any investor on the fast road to riches. What he or she is purchasing, however, is one of the best buy-and-hold stocks available. Again, the dividend has steadily risen for over six decades. And in its many periods of outperformance, Coca-Cola's share price has marched higher, too. We can consider most of this year to be one of those times, and the comparison of total return -- share price appreciation plus dividend payments -- shows the stock trouncing the bellwether S&P 500 index. Witness:

^SPX data by YCharts

How to become a global beverage titan

Coca-Cola likes to hype the lore that the formula for its signature drink is a tightly guarded trade secret known only to a select few. Whether or not that's 100% true, we can say for certain that its formula for commercial success isn't hush-hush at all.

Despite its size, sprawl, and global reach, the company is tightly focused on one key business -- selling a portfolio of beverages anchored by that flagship brown soda. Many Coke-quaffers might not realize that the business behind it owns a bulging portfolio of over 200 drinks, some of which are not, in the public mind, connected to Coca-Cola. Minute Maid orange juice is a company brand, as are Costa Coffee, Gold Peak iced tea, and the implicitly brain-enhancing smartwater.

title: Sandisk’s Stock Split Takes Effect Nov. 19. Should You Buy It Now?
detail:
Sandisk’s Stock Split Takes Effect Nov. 19. Should You Buy It Now?
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 11:05 AM PST 5 min read
SNDK
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has a major event coming soon: a stock split. In the past, stock splits have caused share prices to rise in anticipation of the split, making them popular events to invest in.

However, I think there are far better reasons to invest in Sandisk's stock split, as its business is looking strong. Its stock is also priced quite cheaply, which really makes it a great buy now.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

So, regardless of how the stock reacts after its stock split on Nov. 19, I think Sandisk is a top investment option in the market.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Sandisk is capitalizing on the AI build-out

Sandisk manufactures NAND memory, and also devices that those go into. NAND memory is utilized for long-term data storage and can be used in devices like smartphones and solid-state drives (SSDs). AI hyperscalers and their quest to build out as much computing power as possible have eaten up nearly all production capacity for NAND memory, as they need storage devices like SSDs to store massive amounts of data to be used for AI recall.

That shortage has been a huge boost for Sandisk. There isn't a lot that separates Sandisk's products from the competition, so its clients often went with the cheapest option. However, as supply for these units dried up, prices began to rise. For Sandisk, this isn't a problem, because it can now make a far larger profit on each unit sold because its input costs hadn't changed.

This is reflected in Sandisk's financials, as its gross and profit margins have both soared.

SNDK Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts

This is a major improvement over previous highs and has translated into major shareholder returns. This year, Sandisk is the second-best-performing S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) stock, rising nearly 300% so far in 2026. However, I think it could have more returns ahead of it, as nothing has shifted in the market right now.

Sandisk won't be as cyclical moving forward

The biggest reason why Sandisk and its peers weren't prepared for the AI demand wave is that their clients don't have close working relationships. As mentioned above, its clients utilize the cheapest options available, so that meant bouncing around from supplier to supplier.

Because Sandisk and its peers were operating as cheaply as possible to cut costs, they had no plans to increase production capacity when it wasn't being fully utilized anyway. However, Sandisk's clients have now seen the value in keeping close business ties with them, and Sandisk has started to enter into what it calls "New Business Model" agreements.
